title: SIU: No grounds to charge Hamilton police officer in shooting death of woman
subtitle: Robyn Garlow, 30, was shot twice in a King Street East apartment in October 2018.
article: Ontario's police watchdog says there are no grounds to charge a Hamilton police officer in the shooting death of a 30-year-old woman nearly a year ago.

The woman, identified by family and friends as Robyn Garlow, was pronounced dead at the Hamilton General Hospital around 2 a.m. on Oct. 20, 2018, after being shot twice at a downtown King Street East apartment.

Hamilton police had been called to the apartment, near Wellington Street, around 1 a.m. and found the 30-year-old armed with a knife and "not of sound mind," said Special Investigations Unit interim director Joseph Martino.
He concluded the officer who ultimately fired four shots - two striking her back and chest - was justified.

"I accept that the (subject officer) genuinely and reasonably believed that shooting the complainant was necessary to protect him and his partner from loss of life or grievous bodily harm," Martino said.

The two officers were dispatched to the two-storey apartment building after a 911 call from a neighbour about a woman with a knife. A man, who was in the apartment with Garlow and who had a hammer, had been cut.

When police arrived they were led into the upstairs unit by the cut man and found the 30-year-old woman standing on a bed with a knife in her right hand, the SIU concluded in its director's report released Monday.

Police ordered her to drop the knife, but she refused, brought it up to her neck and started cutting her throat. One officer attempted to Taser the woman twice to stop her from hurting herself, but neither attempt worked.
According to the SIU, the woman then held the knife over her head and was "screaming incomprehensively as she lunged aggressively at the officers."

That's when the other officer pointed his handgun at the woman and "repeatedly" told her to drop the knife, the SIU said. When she continued to move toward the officers he fired four times - two bullets struck her.
She collapsed on the bed and the officer who fired the shots attempted CPR while they waited for an ambulance, but it was too late.
On the number of shots fired, Martino concluded it "would be sheer speculation to draw any meaningful distinction" between one or four shots "given the speed with which events unfolded."
It was a "rapidly developing situation" with less than 30 seconds passing between the officer entering the apartment and shots being fired.
